findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: Chief Executive retiring March 2027 after LGR preparation; Chief Operating Officer post created to manage day-to-day operations from June 2025.
findings.detail: The Chief Executive has been focused on preparing the council for LGR and intends to retire by March 2027. A new Chief Operating Officer post was created and filled by the former Director of Corporate Services to manage day-to-day operations from June 2025. The Chair of the Corporate Governance and Audit Committee changed in May 2026, with Councillor Tim O'Kelly taking over from Councillor Richard Bates, who remains on the committee.
findings.matters: A lender assesses management stability and continuity. Significant changes in senior leadership, particularly the retirement of the Chief Executive during organisational uncertainty (LGR pause), can affect strategic execution and the reliability of financial management.
findings.figures: Chief Executive retiring March 2027; Chief Operating Officer post created June 2025; CGAC Chair changed May 2026.
findings.quote: From June 2025, the Chief Executive's role has focused on preparing the Council for LGR, with the intention to retire by March 2027. The day-to-day running of the Council became the responsibility of a new Chief Operating Officer post, which was filled by the Director of Corporate Services.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: No significant weaknesses identified in arrangements for financial sustainability, governance, or economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
findings.detail: The external auditor completed the Value for Money audit and identified no significant weaknesses in any of the three reporting criteria: financial sustainability, governance, or improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The audit found no risks of significant weakness in the council's arrangements and did not exercise any additional statutory reporting powers. Internal Audit received a 'Generally Achieves' rating in its external quality assessment in December 2025.
findings.matters: A lender seeks assurance that the council has effective controls, financial planning, and governance arrangements. An unqualified VFM opinion indicates the auditor is satisfied with management quality and control environment across all three strategic areas.
findings.figures: No significant weaknesses in any of three criteria; Internal Audit external quality assessment 'Generally Achieves'; no statutory powers exercised.
findings.quote: We did not identify any significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decisions paused for West Sussex area on 7 September 2026.
findings.detail: The government announced a formal review of the LGR programme on 7 September 2026 following legal challenges. West Sussex, including Chichester, was one of 14 areas where a decision was paused. The council had been doing preparatory work for both potential outcomes (single unitary or two unitaries) while awaiting ministerial decision. The pause creates uncertainty around governance, staffing, transformation planning and medium-term financial planning. Local elections due May 2027 will proceed under existing council structures.
findings.matters: A lender must understand governance continuity and the reliability of forward financial plans. Uncertainty over whether the council will exist in its current form within 1–2 years affects credit assessment and the validity of the medium-term financial forecast.
findings.figures: Decisions paused in 14 areas; government review announced 7 September 2026; local elections May 2027 to proceed under existing structures; two options submitted: single unitary or two unitaries.
findings.quote: On 7 September 2026, MHCLG announced a formal review of the Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) programme following legal challenges in four county areas. The Government withdrew previously approved decisions in four areas, paused decisions in a further 14 areas and deferred decisions in two areas where outcomes remained outstanding.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: Usable reserves £119.04m at 31 March 2026, of which £30.42m not earmarked; General Fund £44.24m against minimum approved £4.00m.
findings.detail: The council holds total usable reserves of £119.04m comprising General Fund (£44.24m), Capital Grants Unapplied and Capital Receipts Reserve (£42.92m), and other earmarked reserves (£45.64m). The unearmarked balance of £30.42m provides flexibility to respond to financial pressures. The General Fund is substantially above the minimum approved level of £4.00m (20% of Net Budget Requirement). The chief financial officer reviews reserve adequacy annually and any achieved surplus is transferred to the General Fund to mitigate uncertainty.
findings.matters: A lender requires assurance that the council has adequate liquidity and financial buffers to manage in-year pressures and unexpected costs. The size and composition of reserves indicates financial resilience and the council's capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £119.04m; General Fund £44.24m; Capital Grants Unapplied & Receipts £42.92m; other earmarked reserves £45.64m; unearmarked reserves £30.42m; minimum approved General Fund £4.00m.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: 2025/26 revenue outturn £7.49m surplus, with £6.97m transferred to General Fund Reserve.
findings.detail: The council achieved a £7.49m revenue surplus in 2025/26 against a budgeted position requiring a £0.072m draw from reserves. Of this, £6.97m was transferred to the General Fund Reserve. Major contributors included £2.52m additional investment interest income, £2.00m Extended Producer Responsibility for Packaging grant not in original budget, £1.43m backdated business rates refund for Novium Museum, and £0.58m retrospective rent income, partly offset by £0.41m additional spending on temporary homeless accommodation.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial sustainability by examining reserve trends and the council's ability to deliver budgets. This year shows significant outperformance driven by forecast improvements and non-recurring items including substantial one-off grants and property refunds.
findings.figures: Revenue surplus £7.49m; transfer to General Fund £6.97m; additional interest income £2.52m; EPR grant £2.00m; Novium business rates refund £1.43m; retrospective rent income £0.58m; B&B overspend £0.41m.
findings.quote: The Revenue Outturn showed that the Council was able to achieve a £7.49 million surplus.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: Medium-term financial forecast shifted to surplus for all years 2026/27 to 2030/31 following Fair Funding Review 2.0 grant changes.
findings.detail: The council's November 2025 forecast predicts surplus positions for all five years 2026/27 to 2030/31, a significant shift from the previous forecast showing deficit positions. This change is largely due to updated government grant assumptions following the Fair Funding Review 2.0 (June 2025) and the Local Government Finance Settlement (February 2026). Several grant streams previously expected to end are now rolled into a new Revenue Support Grant valued at £4.3m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's path to sustainability is based on structural improvement or dependent on specific government funding decisions that could change. The shift from expected deficits to surpluses is material to credit assessment.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant £4.3m for 2026/27; forecast surpluses all years 2026/27–2030/31; November 2024 model showed deficits, November 2025 model shows surpluses.
findings.quote: The Council is now predicting surplus positions for all periods in the medium term, compared to the deficit positions included in the previous version of the model.

findings.paper_title: CDC Auditor's Annual Report 2025- 26 - DRAFT October 2026
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion expected for 2025/26; unqualified status achievable when PPE last valued in 2022/23 is revalued.
findings.detail: The council expects a qualified audit opinion for 2025/26, continuing the three-year recovery from disclaimed opinions in 2022/23 and 2023/24. The qualification relates to Property, Plant and Equipment valuations. The auditor can provide only partial assurance over PPE and related reserves until these assets are revalued. The council intends to revalue them in 2027/28, which would defer an unqualified opinion to 2029/30; revaluation in 2026/27 would enable unqualified opinion by 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk must understand the stability of financial reporting. A qualified audit opinion indicates ongoing audit weakness; the timeline for resolution affects the council's ability to demonstrate fully reliable accounts.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions 2022/23 and 2023/24; qualified opinion 2024/25; qualified opinion expected 2025/26; unqualified opinion possible 2028/29 (if PPE revalued 2026/27) or 2029/30 (if revalued 2027/28).
findings.quote: Subject to completion of the remaining outstanding procedures outlined in this report, we expect to issue a qualified opinion.

findings.headline: Council maintains £4m Investment Risk Reserve to cover pooled fund fair value movements
findings.detail: The council has established a £4m Investment Risk Reserve as of September 30, 2026, to protect against potential losses from fair value movements in externally managed pooled funds. Additionally, a statutory override defers recognition of fair value losses in the General Fund until April 1, 2029, for all investments acquired before April 1, 2024.
findings.matters: Shows prudent management of investment portfolio volatility while demonstrating that fair value movements are both reserved for and statutorily shielded from general fund impact in the medium term
findings.figures: £4m reserve; statutory deferral until April 1, 2029
findings.quote: To mitigate potential financial impacts from fair value movements in pooled funds, the Council has maintained an Investment Risk Reserve of £4 million as of September 30, 2026.

findings.headline: Bond maturity restricted to May 2028 due to local government reorganisation; Money Market Funds and Local Authority Investments prioritized for liquidity
findings.detail: The council has deliberately constrained new bond investments to a May 2028 maturity to address uncertainties from potential local government reorganisation. Concurrently, Money Market Fund holdings increased from £10.65m to £16.16m and Local Authority Investments from £51m to £57m, with the council prioritizing short-term liquidity to meet operational needs.
findings.matters: Treasury strategy is adapting to institutional uncertainty while securing liquidity flexibility to manage potential changes; other councils may face similar LGR pressures
findings.figures: Bonds capped at May 2028; MMF increased by £5.51m to £16.16m; LA Investments increased by £6m to £57m
findings.quote: New bonds reinvested recently have not gone beyond May 2028 with the LGR considerations.

findings.headline: Some Section 106 contributions have reached and others are approaching their expenditure deadlines within two years
findings.detail: Developer contributions with spending deadlines are being closely monitored on a quarterly basis and reported to Senior Leadership Team. Spending officers liaise with Ward Members where there is concern about expiry, creating a risk management process around contributions that must be returned to developers if not spent in time.
findings.matters: Developer contributions that expire must be returned to developers, creating a cash flow impact and signalling failure to deliver planned infrastructure; this is a material risk to both project budgets and the council's reputation

findings.headline: Section 106 monitoring operations are not recovering full costs: £25,343 received against £40,789 estimated costs
findings.detail: During 2025/26, monitoring fees of £33,230 were secured and £25,343 received, but estimated monitoring costs are £40,789. This creates a shortfall of at least £7,559 between secured fees and actual costs, and £15,446 between received fees and costs, implying either a subsidy from general funds or cost recovery gaps.
findings.matters: If the council is subsidising the monitoring of developer obligations from general revenue, this is an unbudgeted cost affecting financial position; it also indicates weak contract terms or collection discipline
findings.figures: Monitoring fees secured £33,230; received £25,343; costs estimated £40,789
findings.quote: monitoring fees of £33,230 have been secured and fees of £25,343 received. Monitoring costs are estimated at £40,789.

findings.detail: The unspent S106 balance at year end was £5,588,620, leaving £4,446,208 without specific project allocation (79% unallocated). The paper notes that spending officers are actively engaging with parishes, town councils and other partners regarding the remaining unallocated funds.
findings.matters: Large unallocated developer contributions indicate either weak project planning, slow delivery capacity, or expiry risk; all of which signal infrastructure delivery challenges to a finance director and lender
findings.figures: Total unspent £5,588,620; allocated £1,142,412; unallocated £4,446,208

findings.detail: The council received £8,529,804 in CIL payments during the year against demand notices of £5,365,977. The council handed £1,569,563 to parish and town councils and spent £146,527.96 on CIL administration.
findings.matters: A finance director and external lender need to understand whether approved capital projects are progressing and whether the council can deploy developer contributions at the pace required to fund infrastructure

findings.paper_title: Debt Recovery Update and Annual Debt Write Off Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing debts fell 68% to £109,934 and corporate debts fell to £900,000, both driven by process improvements
findings.detail: Housing debts declined significantly from £344,716 in 2024-25 to £109,934 in 2025-26, a reduction of 68% following a process review focused on maximising benefits entitlement for temporary accommodation tenants. Corporate debt (sundry debts) continued to reduce from £1,060,386 to £900,000. These declines indicate effective debt management in these areas.
findings.matters: Falling arrears driven by process improvements reduce bad debt provision requirements and demonstrate effective financial management, improving overall financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Housing debts 2025-26: £109,934 (down from £344,716 in 2024-25, 68% reduction); Corporate debt 2025-26: £900,000 (down from £1,060,386 in 2024-25)
findings.quote: Housing debts have reduced during 2025/26 following a review of processes. The focus remains on making sure current tenants in our temporary accommodation are assisted and signposted so that benefits entitlement is maximised and thus reduce arrears.

findings.paper_title: Debt Recovery Update and Annual Debt Write Off Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing Benefit overpayment arrears increased by £125,000 in year to £1.46m, attributed to one-off Department of Work and Pensions data matching exercise
findings.detail: Housing Benefit overpayment debt rose from £1,336,684 to £1,461,905, an increase of £125,000. The council attributed this to DWP data matching exercises identifying previously undisclosed capital held by pension-aged claimants. Officers stated they anticipate this represents a one-off adjustment rather than an emerging trend in overpayment recovery.
findings.matters: A lender monitoring council financial position needs to distinguish between one-off accounting adjustments and emerging collection difficulties, as the latter would indicate deteriorating financial sustainability and increasing bad debt provisions.
findings.figures: Housing Benefit overpayment debt: £1,461,905 (2025-26) vs £1,336,684 (2024-25); increase of £125,000
findings.quote: Housing Benefit overpayment debt has increased by £125k during the year. The increase is principally attributable to Department of Work and Pensions data matching exercises which identified previously undisclosed capital held by pension aged claimants. Work by both the Benefits Team and Debt Recovery Team continues and officers anticipate that the increase represents a one-off adjustment rather than an emerging trend.

findings.paper_title: Debt Recovery Update and Annual Debt Write Off Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council Tax arrears nearly doubled from £4.1m to £7.3m in the mid-year position, reflecting cost-of-living pressures, though collection targets were met
findings.detail: Council Tax arrears in the September 2026 position (mid-financial-year) grew from £4,117,136 in 2024-25 to £7,274,026 in 2025-26. The paper attributes this to ongoing cost-of-living pressures and increasing complexity in debt recovery. Despite this growth, the council achieved its 99.5% collection target after post-year-end collections and maintained top 40% national ranking, but the trend shows intensifying financial stress among residents.
findings.matters: Arrears trends indicate underlying financial stress among residents and sustainability of the council's tax base; growing arrears could signal future collection challenges if the pattern of needing post-year-end collection activity to meet targets continues.
findings.figures: Council Tax arrears September 2026: £7,274,026 (2025-26) vs £4,117,136 (2024-25); collection rate achieved: 99.5% (target: 99%)
findings.quote: Despite ongoing cost-of-living pressures and increasing complexity with the debt recovery environment, collection performance remains strong. Council Tax collection remains above 97%

findings.paper_title: Debt Recovery Update and Annual Debt Write Off Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Business Rates collection at 96.44% ranked in lowest 40% of councils nationally, significantly below Council Tax collection of 99.5%
findings.detail: Chichester's Business Rates collection rate in 2025-26 placed it in the lowest 40% of authorities nationally, while its Council Tax collection reached 99.5% and remained in the top 40%. The council attributed Business Rates underperformance to HMRC-controlled retrospective valuation changes and rating appeals outside its control, but the performance gap between the two main income streams is material and indicates concentration of collection risk.
findings.matters: A lender assessing council financial sustainability needs to understand collection performance on both major income streams; significant underperformance in one indicates additional bad debt provision requirements and potential pressure on financial resilience.
findings.figures: Business Rates 96.44% (lowest 40% nationally); Council Tax 99.5% collection achieved post-year-end and 97.07% at 31 March 2026 (top 40% nationally)

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant projected to decline 28% from £4.288m (2026-27) to £3.066m (2028-29), then recover to £3.831m (2029-30)
findings.detail: Revenue Support Grant is projected to fall from £4,288k in 2026-27 to £3,066k by 2028-29 (a 28% decline of £1,222k), before recovering to £3,831k in 2029-30 and stabilizing at £3,873k through 2031-32. The plan does not explain what policy change, distribution formula shift, or other mechanism underlies this volatility or recovery assumption. The sharp recovery from 2029-30 is load-bearing to the five-year plan but lacks stated justification.
findings.matters: Unexplained government funding volatility, particularly an assumed recovery, creates forecast risk; if the recovery does not materialise or is delayed, the council's return to surplus and reserve rebuild fails.

These represent permanent reductions in service capacity unless absorptions or replacements are in place.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Council reduces assumed council tax collection rate from 99% to 98.5% from 2027-28, creating £62-£70k recurring budget pressure
findings.detail: The plan explicitly reduces the assumed council tax collection rate from 99% to 98.5% from 2027-28 onwards, widening the assumed non-collection from 1% to 1.5% of the tax base. This creates an incremental budget pressure of £62k in 2027-28, growing to £70k by 2031-32 as the tax base grows. The reduction signals either emerging real concerns about collection rates or a prudent downward adjustment from prior-year assumptions.
findings.matters: Collection rate assumptions are fundamental to cash flow forecasting; a reduction either indicates emerging collection problems or reflects a policy shift toward more conservative assumptions.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Housing services carry persistent £1.6m annual cost pressure from 2027-28 onwards with no offsetting savings plan
findings.detail: Housing is identified as a 'Must Do' service-specific cost pressure of £1,625k in 2026-27 and £1,646k annually from 2027-28 through 2031-32, making it the largest single service pressure in the plan. This appears driven by homelessness and housing support statutory duties (the plan separately shows 'Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and Domestic Abuse Grant' items). Unlike other service pressures, housing has no corresponding efficiency savings line to offset the cost growth.
findings.matters: This is structural demand growth in a statutory service with no reduction plan; it represents an unfunded pressure that could force service rationing or additional reserve draw if planned efficiency savings fall short.
findings.figures: Housing cost pressure: 1,625 (2026-27) / 1,646 annually (2027-28 through 2031-32)

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Plan depends on efficiency savings and income improvements of £2.4m-£3.1m annually from 2028-29 onwards to achieve surplus and reserve recovery
findings.detail: The financial model assumes efficiency savings and income improvements starting at £48k in 2026-27, rising to £952k in 2027-28, then stepping up to £2,404k in 2028-29 and growing to £3,147k by 2031-32. Growth and Place service is projected to deliver £1,375k to £1,903k of these savings annually from 2028-29 onwards. Without these materialisations, the council cannot move from deficit to surplus and cannot rebuild reserves as planned.
findings.matters: The transition from deficit to surplus and the reserve recovery are entirely dependent on this specific efficiency savings trajectory; shortfalls or delays in Growth and Place delivery would create a structural budget gap.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 2
findings.headline: Cumulative reserve draw-down peaks at £2.9m in 2027-28, recovers to £868k by 2029-30, then reverses to rebuild of £5.7m by 2031-32
findings.detail: The plan shows cumulative net reserve draw-down of £2,326k in 2026-27, rising to £2,881k by 2027-28 (peak draw), then gradually recovering to £868k by 2029-30 as deficits narrow. From 2030-31 onwards, the position reverses: cumulative reserves move into surplus, reaching £2,115k rebuild by 2030-31 and £5,696k by 2031-32. This represents a three-year vulnerability period where reserves decline, followed by planned recovery dependent on achieving the projected surpluses.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion creates vulnerability to shocks; lenders and peer councils assess both the scale and timing of draw-down and whether the recovery plan is credible given other budget pressures.

findings.paper_title: Chichester District Council - EY 2025.26 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: Management must complete reconciliation of disclaimed-period reserves and provide capacity to support historic rebuild without compromising current year audit delivery
findings.detail: Before audit commences, management must complete robust review and reconciliation of all usable and unusable reserves for disclaimed periods (2022/23 and earlier where applicable) and provide assurance to governance that balances are accurate, supportable and documented. EY requires high-quality working papers and supporting evidence for historic transactions, with management confirmation of sufficient capacity to execute rebuild without compromising 2025/26 audit procedures on closing balances and in-year movements.
findings.matters: The rebuild depends on management's ability to locate and present historic evidence and sustain resource commitment. Insufficient capacity or gaps in documentation could delay progression to unqualified opinion. This is an operational constraint directly affecting the timeline and feasibility of audit recovery.
findings.figures: Risk assessment covered 2022/23 and earlier years where applicable

findings.paper_title: Chichester District Council - EY 2025.26 - LG Reserve Risk Assessment Update Report
findings.headline: Qualified audit opinion expected to continue in 2025/26, with progression to unqualified dependent on revaluation of material property, plant and equipment last valued in the original disclaimed year 2022/23
findings.detail: The council received a qualified (except for) audit opinion in 2024/25 following disclaimer opinions for 2023/24. EY's risk assessment indicates a qualified (except for) opinion is expected in 2025/26. Progression to unqualified opinion is contingent on revaluation of material PPE last valued in 2022/23. The council operates a rolling five-year valuation program; material PPE from 2022/23 will remain unvalued at end of 2025/26 unless the cycle is accelerated.
findings.matters: The audit opinion is the foundation of external assurance on financial statements. This identifies the specific operational constraint blocking audit recovery: the council's own PPE valuation schedule. Other councils with multi-year rolling revaluation programs face the same timing risk, making this outcome material to how peers plan asset revaluation cycles post-disclaimer.
findings.figures: 2022/23 original disclaimed year; rolling 5-year programme; material value of PPE
findings.quote: At the end of 2025/26 a material value of PPE last valued in 2022/23, the original disclaimed year, has not been subsequently revalued. We do not have assurance over the valuation of that PPE and associated movements in income and expenditure. Our ability to move forward from a qualified (except for) opinion is therefore dependent on when that PPE is next subject to valuation.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 Appendix 3
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves of 44,242 are deployed to fund capital programme at 17,215 in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has 44,242 in earmarked reserves designated for capital projects. In 2026/27, 17,215 of these reserves are applied to fund current capital projects. findings.headline: Local Plan 2045 delivery at high risk with three current vacancies and one anticipated 12-month absence in planning team
findings.detail: The Local Plan 2045 has a high risk score of 9 with no improvement toward the target of 6. The planning team is running with three current vacancies (1 Principal Planning Officer and 2 Planning Officers) with a further Principal Planning Officer absence anticipated for up to 1 year. Internal control status for 'Sufficient staff resources to achieve timetable' is rated 'Poor'. The uncertain Local Government Reorganisation timeline compounds the difficulty.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver a current Local Plan means loss of planning control and presumption in favour of development; peers watch how councils maintain planning certainty during austerity and organizational change.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation paused with likely delay of at least one year; council risk score increased from 6 to 9
findings.detail: The government paused the Local Government Reorganisation programme on 7 September 2026, creating significant uncertainty. The council had been planning for reorganization but now must prepare for district elections on existing boundaries in 2027 instead. The risk score has increased from 6 to 9, reflecting heightened uncertainty about reorganization timeline and whether Chichester will move into a unitary with Horsham, Crawley and Mid Sussex.
findings.matters: This fundamentally affects the council's financial planning, organizational structure and resource allocation; lenders and peers would want to know whether councils are maintaining separate planning for multiple scenarios and what financial impact the uncertainty carries.
findings.figures: Risk score 6→9 (target 4 by 31-Mar-2028); likely delay of at least one year to programme
findings.quote: it is now extremely likely that there will be a delay to the programme of at least one year and we have been told to prepare for the elections scheduled for 2027 on the existing boundaries (District elections in our case).

findings.headline: Food waste collection service delivered on time and within budget in March 2026, reaching 90% household coverage
findings.detail: The council successfully implemented the statutory weekly food waste collection service in March 2026, on the target date of 31 March 2026. Collections were phased between 23 March and 4 May 2026, reaching approximately 90% of households. The project was delivered within budget and risk score reduced from 6 to 2, meeting the target.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council's ability to execute a major statutory service change on time and within budget; peers note this as evidence of effective project delivery capability under tight timescales.
findings.figures: Risk score 6→2 (target achieved 31-Mar-2026); 90% household coverage
findings.quote: The risk has substantially reduced following the successful launch of the household food waste collection service in March 2026, in line with the project timetable.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand risk remains at score 9 despite increased investment in staffing and funding
findings.detail: The Homelessness Service Demand risk score remains at 9 (original 9, previous 9, current 9), with no improvement toward the target of 4. The council has created an additional post, maintained full staffing levels, and allocated an additional £100k to the Discretionary Housing Fund to meet ongoing demand driven by the cost-of-living crisis. Despite these measures, the risk has not reduced, suggesting sustained financial pressure.
findings.matters: Finance directors and peers monitor how councils manage sustained demand pressures from cost-of-living impacts; the fact that this risk score is not reducing despite increased resources suggests ongoing budget pressure on the homelessness service.
findings.figures: Risk score 9→9→9 (target 4 by 31-Mar-2027); additional post created; additional £100k allocated to Discretionary Housing Fund
findings.quote: The Divisional Manager continues to closely monitor this risk and respond to both local and national challenges.

findings.headline: Selsey coastal defence risk score reduced from 12 to 8 as Environment Agency funding secured for urgent West Beach works
findings.detail: The council has secured Environment Agency funding for urgent coastal defence works at West Beach and completed repair works at Sea Grove costing £60k. Construction is scheduled to begin 24 August 2026 with 12-week completion. The risk had been the potential for major unfunded emergency repairs along the Selsey frontage; the risk score improvement from 12 to 8 reflects mitigation of this liability.
findings.matters: This represents mitigation of a material unfunded liability risk; a lender would see the securing of grant funding as reducing the council's exposure to major unplanned capital expenditure.
findings.figures: Risk score 12→8 (target 2 by 31-Aug-2030); £60k repair at Sea Grove completed; urgent works funding obtained from EA
findings.quote: Funding from the EA has now been obtained, as has planning permission and a Marine Management Organisation license.  Construction is due to start on 24 August 2026, with completion in 12 weeks, weather allowing.

findings.headline: Council maintains strong financial position with significant reserves, is debt-free, and has set a £34.1m capital programme for 2026-27
findings.detail: The council remains in a strong financial position with significant reserves and liquid investments available to respond to financial shocks. It is debt-free but can access the PWLB if required. A 3-year settlement announced in December 2026 provides certainty for funding through 2028-29. The Financial Resilience risk score has improved from the original 9 to the current 4, tracking toward the target of 3 by March 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director or peer would want to know whether the council is building financial resilience or drawing down its position; a lender would want to see debt-free status and available liquidity.
findings.figures: Capital programme £34.1m (2026-27); risk score 9→4 (target 3 by 31-Mar-2027)
findings.quote: The Council remains in a strong financial position having significant reserves and the ability to call upon its substantial liquid investments if required, demonstrating its agility to react to any financial shocks.

findings.headline: Four of 15 strategic risks lack controls; only 11 have controls adequately in place
findings.detail: Of the 15 strategic risks identified, 11 are considered to have controls that are adequately in place. The remaining 4 risks have controls that are still pending, meaning mitigation actions are in progress but not yet fully implemented.
findings.matters: Mature governance requires controls to be implemented, not pending. The existence of 4 controls still being developed indicates that some aspects of risk management are incomplete, signalling governance maturity and capability challenges.
findings.figures: 11 of 15 risks adequately controlled; 4 with controls pending
findings.quote: Of these, 11 are considered to be adequately controlled, while the remaining 4 have controls pending

findings.headline: Selsey sea defences risk score improved from 12 to 8
findings.detail: The risk score for Managing Selsey's Aging Sea Defences has decreased from 12 to 8. This represents progress in managing what was previously the highest-scored risk on the strategic register, suggesting either successful mitigation or better understanding of the challenge.
findings.matters: Coastal defence liabilities represent material long-term financial exposure. Risk improvement indicates either successful mitigation or better management, reducing uncertainty and potential future financial demands on the council.
findings.figures: Risk score decreased from 12 to 8

findings.detail: Two new strategic risks have been identified focused on governance: Corporate Compliance (initial score 4) and Failure of Ethical Governance Standards (initial score 6). These new risks indicate the council has identified areas in governance and compliance that require management attention.
findings.matters: Governance failures or compliance issues affect council credibility and operations. New explicit governance risks signal areas the council has identified as requiring focus. For lenders, governance quality is a material assessment factor.
findings.figures: CRR 203 score 4, CRR 204 score 6

findings.headline: Local Plan 2045 identified as new strategic risk with initial score of 9

This reflects the council's assessment that the plan represents a significant management challenge.
findings.matters: The local plan is fundamental to the council's long-term growth strategy and financial sustainability. A high-risk rating indicates substantial uncertainty or challenges in delivery, which affects development income and economic resilience.
findings.figures: Initial score 9
findings.quote: CRR 205 - local Plan 2045 (with an initial scan of 9)

findings.headline: Legal Services resource shortage escalated to score 9
findings.detail: The risk score for Legal Services—specifically the lack of team resources to deliver projects and day-to-day business—has escalated from 6 to 9. This is the only score change reported among the council's organisational risks, indicating significant resource constraint in a core service.
findings.matters: Resource constraints in legal services affect capacity to deliver capital projects, manage contracts, and maintain governance. Lenders monitor service capacity as a delivery risk indicator; peer councils are experiencing similar staffing pressures.

findings.detail: The risk score for Local Government Reorganisation has increased significantly from 6 to 9. This represents one of only two score changes among the 15 strategic risks and reflects the council's assessment of uncertainty around potential local government structural or boundary changes.
findings.matters: Reorganisation could fundamentally alter the council's structure, governance, and finances. Lenders require certainty about council stability; peer finance directors are tracking the same organisational uncertainty across the sector.

findings.detail: The proposed reorganisation of West Sussex local government has paused following government announcement to review decisions already taken. No timeline provided for review or implementation. Council is preparing 2027-28 budget on business-as-usual basis to protect financial stability. Timing and nature of capital projects and revenue growth are being considered in light of potential LGR, with aim that decisions do not fetter successor authority's financial position.
findings.matters: LGR creates uncertainty that prevents definitive multi-year planning. Council is taking cautious approach to avoid building commitments that could constrain a successor authority, but this also creates constraints for current council. Finance directors at other councils face similar uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Financial Strategy and Plan 2027-28 to 2031-32 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Interest income policy updated to allow use for revenue expenditure if reserves drawdown becomes necessary
findings.detail: In 2026-27, the council updated its key financial principle for Capital Receipts and Reserves to allow interest income on investments to be used for both capital projects and revenue expenditure if necessary. Previously, only income from long-term multi-asset funds was routinely applied to revenue. This change provides flexibility to balance revenue budget using investment income as an alternative to reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Policy change indicates the council is adjusting financial management to access more flexible funding sources. Use of volatile interest income to support recurring revenue is generally considered less prudent than revenue-based solutions, suggesting the council is managing budget strain.
findings.figures: Policy updated in 2026-27
findings.quote: In 2026-27 the key principle for Capital Receipts and Reserves was updated to allow for interest on investments to be used for both capital projects and revenue expenditure if necessary

findings.headline: Budget forecast to return to surplus from 2028-29 onwards, primarily from new leisure centre management contract revenue

The model indicates an underlying surplus of approximately £0.324m to £3.581m across 2027-28 through to 2031-32, showing return to sustainable position once temporary pressures ease.

However, return to balance depends on the leisure centre contract performing as expected, which represents a key assumption and risk. findings.detail: The council's approved five-year capital and asset replacement programme totalling £43.763m (excluding Community Infrastructure Levy schemes) remains fully funded without requirement for external borrowing. An additional £9.155m of uncommitted resources is available for new projects and service investment over the medium term, subject to the use of investment interest income for revenue support.
findings.matters: Indicates the council's capital investment is sustainable without requiring borrowing. findings.quote: The current approved 5 year capital and asset renewal programmes totalling £43.763m (excluding CIL schemes) remains fully funded without the need to borrow from external sources

findings.detail: The Business Rate Retention Scheme was reset as part of the 2026-27 settlement to target funding where most needed. For Chichester, this reset eliminated all business rates growth generated since localisation began, resulting in a structural reduction in baseline funding of £2.46m from 2025-26 to 2026-27.
findings.matters: This is a structural loss of baseline funding, not a cyclical shortfall. Such permanent reductions reduce council revenue capacity and require offsetting savings or service reductions. Finance directors at peer councils face similar impacts; lenders assess these as permanent reductions to council capacity.

The council states it is imperative to develop alternative means of provision to mitigate costs and achieve better value. Risk assessment rates this as high probability with £0.8m potential impact; alternative provision approaches rated medium probability with £0.8m saving potential.
findings.matters: This is a demand-driven cost pressure affecting multiple councils. The scale (£0.8m on a budget base of ~£19m) is material. Mitigations are uncertain (medium probability), making this a key risk for finance directors watching peer councils and for lenders assessing budget stability.

findings.quote: By far the most significant financial pressure facing the Council is the increasing cost of providing commercially sourced night-time accommodation to those in need, as demand for these services continues to grow.

Combined with identified cost pressures, the total estimated movement on reserves to balance the 2026-27 budget is £7.088m. The council expects to use investment interest income and/or reserves to balance the budget in the short term. Recovery to surplus is expected from 2028-29 onwards.
findings.matters: Budget deficits indicate the council cannot cover costs from current income and must use reserves or interest income to balance. Finance directors at peer councils and lenders assess budget sustainability through multi-year deficit periods.

These represent a pattern of significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance requiring improvement across multiple service and corporate areas.

findings.matters: Income volatility in a material council revenue stream signals budget pressure and forecast risk; recovery potential from policy changes is material to whether the shortfall is temporary.

findings.headline: Legal services risk score escalated to 9 as two solicitors depart and locum cover remains only part-time
findings.detail: The legal team's risk score has increased from 6 to 9, driven by departures of the Contracts Solicitor and Litigation Solicitor. findings.matters: Staffing shortages and locum costs represent unbudgeted spend and service continuity risk; a finance director watching peer council staffing pressures would note whether additional establishment costs are coming.

findings.quote: Current workload and instructions exceed capacity...Two departures from the team – the Contracts solicitor and Litigation Solicitor – have meant that locum provision has been needed to cover the work needed.
